--- lecture: "07b" metadata-files: - ../../_slide-settings.yml format: revealjs: theme: default --- ::: {.my-title} # [Statistical Methods]{.blue} One-way ANOVA / Effect Sizes / Contrasts ::: {.my-grey} [{{< meta semester >}} | Course {{< meta course >}}]{}
[{{< meta instructor >}} | Lecture {{< meta lecture >}}]{} ::: ::: {.my-attrib} {{< meta attribution >}} ::: ![](../../img/statistics_2780E3.png){.absolute bottom=30 right=0 width="400"} ::: ::: {.cell} ::: # Introduction ## Rationale - The $t$-test compares two groups' population means - But sometimes we want to compare **three or more** groups - This is what [one-way analysis of variance]{.b .blue} (ANOVA) does + One-way focuses on *one* source of variance (i.e., groups) + The one-way ANOVA is for **independent samples**/groups $$ H_0: \text{it is true that } \mu_1=\mu_2=\mu_3 \cdots \\ H_1: \text{it is NOT true that } \mu_1=\mu_2=\mu_3 \cdots $$ ## Example dataset ::: {.cell replace_path='["../../data/",""]'} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) salaries <- read_csv("../../data/salaries.csv") salaries ## # A tibble: 397 × 6 ## rank discipline yrs.since.phd yrs.service sex salary ## ## 1 Full Applied 19 18 Male 140. ## 2 Full Applied 20 16 Male 173. ## 3 Assistant Applied 4 3 Male 79.8 ## 4 Full Applied 45 39 Male 115 ## 5 Full Applied 40 41 Male 142. ## 6 Associate Applied 6 6 Male 97 ## 7 Full Applied 30 23 Male 175 ## 8 Full Applied 45 45 Male 148. ## 9 Full Applied 21 20 Male 119. ## 10 Full Applied 18 18 Female 129 ## # ℹ 387 more rows ``` ::: - Do the three professor **ranks** have the same mean salary? ## Exploratory analysis ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](b_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## Total variance *Across all observations (in all groups), what is the average squared difference between each observation and the global mean (calculated across all observations in all groups)?* $$ \text{Var}(y)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i - \bar{y})^2 $$ $n$ is the total sample size across all groups $\bar{y}$ is the global mean of $y$ across all groups ## Sums of squares - ANOVA uses [sums of squares]{.b .blue} ($SS$) rather than variances + $SS$ are the same as variances but don't divide by $n$ + They are the **sums** of squared differences (not the means) ::: {.columns} ::: {.column} $$\color{blue}{\text{SS}_{tot}=\sum_{i=1}^n(y_{i}-\bar{y})^2}$$ ::: ::: {.column} $$\text{Var}(y)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n(y_{i} - \bar{y})^2$$ ::: ::: ::: {.footer} Using $SS$ yields a nicer interpretation and enables the use of the $F$ distribution ::: ## Between and within groups - The total variation ($SS_{tot}$) contains two components ![](../../img/between_within.png) ::: {.columns} ::: {.column} *How different are the three groups/ranks (on average)?* ::: ::: {.column} *How different are professors
in the same group/rank?* ::: ::: ## Decomposing the variation - We can decompose total variation into two components: ::: {.columns} ::: {.column} **Between-group variation** $$\text{SS}_b = \sum_{k=1}^gn_k(\bar{y}_k - \bar{y})^2$$ *How far is each group mean $\bar{y}_k$ from the global mean $\bar{y}$?* ::: ::: {.column} **Within-group variation** $$\text{SS}_w = \sum_{k=1}^g\sum_{i=1}^{n_k}(y_{ik} - \bar{y}_k)^2$$ *How far is each observation $y_{ik}$ from its group mean $\bar{y}_k$?* ::: ::: ::: {.footer} Note that the decomposition ensures that $SS_{tot}=SS_b + SS_w$ ::: ## Testing for mean differences - If $H_0$ is true, the groups' population means are the same + Thus, between-group variation $(SS_b)$ should be small ::: {.fragment} - But how small is small enough? We need to contextualize it + ANOVA does so by comparing $SS_b$ to $SS_w$ + It focuses on the ratio of $SS_b$ to $SS_w$ (i.e., $SS_b/SS_w$) + But we need to build in the group and sample sizes + Doing so will allow us to calibrate our uncertainty ::: ## Incorporating uncertainty ::: {.tc} ::: {.columns} ::: {.column} **Mean Squares Between** $$\textit{MS}_b = \frac{\textit{SS}_b}{g - 1}$$ ::: ::: {.column} **Mean Squares Within** $$\textit{MS}_w = \frac{\textit{SS}_w}{n - g}$$ ::: ::: [The One-way ANOVA Test Statistic]{.b} $$ F_{obs} = \frac{\textit{MS}_b}{\textit{MS}_w}\\ F_{obs} \sim F(\textit{df}_1 = g - 1, \textit{df}_2 = n - g) $$ ::: ::: {.footer} $g$ is the number of groups, $n$ is the total sample size ::: ## The F distribution ::: {.columns} ::: {.column} - The sum of squared normally distributed values will have a $\chi^2$ distribution - The ratio of two $\chi^2$ distributed variables will have an $F$ distribution $$x \sim F(\textit{df}_1, \textit{df}_2)$$ ::: ::: {.column} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](b_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){width=576} ::: ::: ::: ::: ## The df1 parameter ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](b_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){width=1152} ::: ::: - Higher $\textit{df}_1$ has thinner tails (i.e., lower critical values) ## The df2 parameter ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](b_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){width=1152} ::: ::: - Higher $\textit{df}_2$ has thinner tails (i.e., lower critical values) # One-way ANOVA in R ## The aov function - The `aov()` function will do this math for us ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fit <- aov( formula = salary ~ rank, data = salaries ) ``` ::: ::: {.fragment .pv4} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} summary(fit) ## Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F) ## rank 2 143232 71616 128.2 <2e-16 *** ## Residuals 394 220069 559 ## --- ## Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Critical value (to compare to F_obs = 128.2) qf(.975, df1 = 2, df2 = 394) ## [1] 3.723634 ``` ::: ::: ## Prettier output ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(easystats) model_parameters(fit) ## Parameter | Sum_Squares | df | Mean_Square | F | p ## ------------------------------------------------------------- ## rank | 1.43e+05 | 2 | 71615.88 | 128.22 | < .001 ## Residuals | 2.20e+05 | 394 | 558.55 | | ## ## Anova Table (Type 1 tests) ``` ::: *We used a one-way ANOVA to compare the mean salaries of Assistant, Associate, and Full professors and rejected the null hypothesis that these three groups have the same mean, $F(2,394)=128.22$, $p<.001$.* ## Estimating group means - We can also estimate the model-implied group means ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} gmeans <- estimate_means(fit, by = "rank") gmeans ## Estimated Marginal Means ## ## rank | Mean | SE | 95% CI | t(394) ## ----------------------------------------------------- ## Assistant | 80.78 | 2.89 | [ 75.10, 86.45] | 27.98 ## Associate | 93.88 | 2.95 | [ 88.07, 99.68] | 31.78 ## Full | 126.77 | 1.45 | [123.92, 129.62] | 87.48 ## ## Variable predicted: salary ## Predictors modulated: rank ``` ::: ::: {.footer} Note that this function requires the {emmeans} package to be installed ::: ## Plotting group means ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot(gmeans) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](b_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-13-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## An effect size for One-way ANOVA - We conclude that $H_0$ is wrong, but *how wrong* was it? - **How much of the total variation was between groups?** $$\eta^2 = \frac{SS_b}{SS_{tot}}$$ - If $\eta^2=0$, then none of the variation was between groups - If $\eta^2=1$, then all of the variation was between groups ## Application and interpretation ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ss_b <- 143232 ss_w <- 220069 ss_tot <- ss_b + ss_w ss_b / ss_tot ## [1] 0.3942516 ``` ::: ::: {.pv4} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} eta_squared(fit) ## # Effect Size for ANOVA ## ## Parameter | Eta2 | 95% CI ## ------------------------------- ## rank | 0.39 | [0.33, 1.00] ## ## - One-sided CIs: upper bound fixed at [1.00]. ``` ::: ::: - So 39% of the variation in salary was between groups/ranks # Post-hoc Tests ## Many ways to reject the null - Recall that our null hypothesis is that $\mu_1=\mu_2=\mu_3$ ::: {.fs60} | Possibility | $\mu_1=\mu_2$ | $\mu_1=\mu_3$ | $\mu_2=\mu_3$ | Hypothesis | | ----------- | ------------- | ------------- | ------------- | ----------- | | 1 | TRUE | TRUE | TRUE | null | | 2 | - | TRUE | TRUE | alternative | | 3 | TRUE | - | TRUE | alternative | | 4 | TRUE | TRUE | - | alternative | | 5 | TRUE | - | - | alternative | | 6 | - | TRUE | - | alternative | | 7 | - | - | TRUE | alternative | | 8 | - | - | - | alternative | ::: - Thus, if we reject the null, we don't know exactly why... ## Pairwise $t$-tests - To figure it out, we can run a $t$-test for each pair of groups + These are called "post hoc" (Latin for "after that") tests $$\mu_1=\mu_2 \qquad \mu_1=\mu_3 \qquad \mu_2=\mu_3$$ - There are two main challenges with this approach + It will be a hassle to run all these tests as $g$ increases + Running many tests will increase the Type I Error rate ## Addressing the challenges - For the first challenge, we will use programming + We will use R functions to do all the work for us - For the second challenge, we will use two approaches + **Gating:** only run post-hoc tests if ANOVA is significant + $p$-value adjustment: increase $p$ based on \# of tests run - We want to keep the overall ("familywise") error rate at $\alpha$ + We will learn two common adjustment approaches ## Bonferroni correction - Multiply each $p$ by the number of tests run ($m$) $$p' = p \times m$$ ::: {.fs70} | raw $p$ | $m$ | Bonferroni $p'$ | | ----------- | --- | --------------- | | .001 \*\*\* | 5 | .005 \*\* | | .005 \*\* | 5 | .025 \* | | .019 \* | 5 | .095 | | .022 \* | 5 | .110 | | .103 | 5 | .515 | ::: ::: {.footer} Bonferonni is simple but very conservative ::: ## Holm correction - Pretend you do the tests from smallest to largest $p$-value - Take the larger of $(p'_j=j\times p_j)$ and $(p'_{j+1})$ :::{.fs70} | raw $p$ | rank $j$ | $p\times j$ | Holm $p'$ | | ----------- | -------- | ----------- | -------- | | .001 \*\*\* | 5 | .005 | .005 \*\* | | .005 \*\* | 4 | .020 | .020 \* | | .019 \* | 3 | .057 | .057 | | .022 \* | 2 | .044 | .057 | | .103 | 1 | .103 | .103 | ::: ::: {.footer} Holm is complicated but more powerful ::: ## Post-hoc tests in R ::: {.fs90} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} estimate_contrasts( model = fit, contrast = "rank", method = "pairwise", p_adjust = "bonferroni" ) ## Marginal Contrasts Analysis ## ## Level1 | Level2 | Difference | SE | 95% CI | t(394) | p ## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- ## Associate | Assistant | 13.10 | 4.13 | [ 4.98, 21.22] | 3.17 | 0.005 ## Full | Assistant | 46.00 | 3.23 | [39.64, 52.35] | 14.24 | < .001 ## Full | Associate | 32.90 | 3.29 | [26.43, 39.36] | 10.00 | < .001 ## ## Variable predicted: salary ## Predictors contrasted: rank ## p-value adjustment method: Bonferroni ``` ::: ::: ## Adjustment in R ::: {.fs90} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} estimate_contrasts( model = fit, contrast = "rank", method = "pairwise", p_adjust = "holm" # change the method here ) ## Marginal Contrasts Analysis ## ## Level1 | Level2 | Difference | SE | 95% CI | t(394) | p ## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- ## Associate | Assistant | 13.10 | 4.13 | [ 4.98, 21.22] | 3.17 | 0.002 ## Full | Assistant | 46.00 | 3.23 | [39.64, 52.35] | 14.24 | < .001 ## Full | Associate | 32.90 | 3.29 | [26.43, 39.36] | 10.00 | < .001 ## ## Variable predicted: salary ## Predictors contrasted: rank ## p-value adjustment method: Holm (1979) ``` ::: :::

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
